title: “OBEY YOUR LEADERS AND SUBMIT TO THEM” — BUT WHAT IF YOUR LEADER IS LEADING YOU AWAY FROM CHRIST?
paragraphs: “OBEY YOUR LEADERS AND SUBMIT TO THEM” — BUT WHAT IF YOUR LEADER IS LEADING YOU AWAY FROM CHRIST?

Hebrews 13:17 has been used to silence questions, demand loyalty, and frighten wounded believers into submission. But what did the Holy Spirit actually mean? The answer may confront abusive leadership, challenge rebellious hearts, and set exhausted Christians free to follow Jesus without abandoning His Church.
There is a kind of pain that only happens inside a church.
It is the pain of trusting someone who taught you about Jesus… only to discover that the same person could use the name of Jesus to control you.
It is the confusion of sitting beneath a pulpit, hearing the Word of God preached, while quietly wondering why asking an honest question suddenly makes you rebellious.
It is the fear of being called disobedient when all you wanted was to understand Scripture.

And sometimes, it is the loneliness of realizing that the people who taught you to recognize the voice of the Good Shepherd are now demanding that you stop questioning the voice of the shepherd standing in front of you.
Perhaps you have been there.
Perhaps you were told, “Touch not the Lord's anointed.”
Perhaps someone warned you that questioning your pastor was equivalent to questioning God.
Perhaps you were pressured to give money you could not afford, remain silent about something you knew was wrong, or accept decisions that wounded your conscience.
And when you finally found the courage to speak, someone opened a Bible and read Hebrews 13:17.
“Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account…” (Hebrews 13:17, KJV).
Then came the sentence that broke something inside you.
“God said you must obey.”
But here is the question that deserves an answer from Scripture, not intimidation:
Does God command Christians to obey spiritual leaders even when those leaders are wrong?
And here is an equally important question:
What happens when a Christian uses the failures of church leaders as an excuse to reject every form of spiritual accountability?
Because this passage confronts both dangers.
The leader who wants unquestioned power.
And the believer who refuses godly correction.
One can turn the church into a place of control.
The other can turn Christian freedom into spiritual isolation.
Neither reflects the heart of Jesus Christ.
And if we are going to understand Hebrews 13:17, we must allow Scripture to speak even when its answer challenges the people we admire, the traditions we inherited, and the wounds we carry.
The truth is more beautiful, more demanding, and more liberating than either blind obedience or complete independence.
It begins with a Greek word.
The New Testament was written in Koine Greek, and Hebrews 13:17 opens with a command:
Πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν καὶ ὑπείκετε.
Peithesthe tois hēgoumenois hymōn kai hypeikete.
The traditional English rendering is:
“Obey your leaders and submit to them.”
But the Greek deserves careful attention.
The word translated “obey” is πείθεσθε (peithesthe), from the verb πείθω (peithō).
This verb can carry meanings connected with persuading, convincing, trusting, and obeying. In this grammatical form and context, it is appropriately translated “obey,” “be persuaded by,” or “heed.”
That does not mean the command is optional.
It does mean we should not automatically imagine the kind of obedience demanded by a dictator who forbids questions.
The verse addresses believers who are expected to respond to legitimate spiritual leadership, receive sound instruction, and cooperate with those entrusted with caring for them.
Then comes the second command.
Ὑπείκετε (hypeikete).
It means to yield, give way, or submit.
The writer is calling Christians to a genuine willingness to cooperate with their spiritual leaders.
Not merely to listen when the sermon feels encouraging.
Not merely to respect leaders when every decision agrees with personal preferences.
Real submission involves humility.
It sometimes requires accepting correction.
It sometimes means setting aside personal pride for the good of the church.
But notice something important.
Neither Greek word makes a human leader infallible.
And neither command erases the authority of Jesus Christ.
The verse continues:
αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἀγρυπνοῦσιν ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν
Autoi gar agrypnousin hyper tōn psychōn hymōn.
“For they keep watch over your souls.”
The word ἀγρυπνοῦσιν (agrypnousin) describes keeping awake, remaining watchful, or maintaining vigilance.
Think about that.
The picture is not of a king sitting comfortably on a throne, demanding that everyone bow.
It is of someone remaining awake because others have been entrusted to their care.
A faithful shepherd notices when a sheep is wandering.
A faithful shepherd warns when danger approaches.
A faithful shepherd does not celebrate having power over vulnerable people.
He understands the weight of being responsible for their spiritual well-being.
And the verse adds something that should make every pastor, elder, ministry leader, and spiritual mentor tremble:
ὡς λόγον ἀποδώσοντες
Hōs logon apodōsontes.
“As those who will give an account.”
An account to whom?
Ultimately, to God.
That changes everything.
Hebrews 13:17 is not simply a command directed toward church members.
It is also a solemn reminder that spiritual leaders are accountable for the way they exercise their responsibilities.
The pastor is not the owner of the sheep.
The elder is not the savior of the congregation.
The ministry leader is not the final authority over another person's conscience.
Jesus Christ is the Chief Shepherd.
And every under-shepherd must answer to Him.
Peter understood this.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, he instructed elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not as those who dominate the people entrusted to them, but as examples.
The Greek expression translated “being lords over” is connected with κατακυριεύω (katakyrieuō), meaning to exercise mastery or dominion over others.
Peter explicitly warns against that kind of leadership.
And he does not stop there.
In 1 Peter 5:4, he points to the appearing of the Chief Shepherd.
The message is unmistakable.
The flock belongs to God.
Leadership is stewardship.
Authority is responsibility.
And spiritual oversight is never permission to dominate the people Jesus purchased with His blood.
Imagine a pastor standing before Christ.
Not standing before a congregation that applauds every sermon.
Not standing before a social media audience impressed by his influence.
Not standing before a ministry board that measures success only by attendance, donations, and buildings.
Standing before Jesus.
The One who sees what happened behind closed doors.
The One who heard the conversations nobody recorded.
The One who knows whether a struggling believer was gently restored or publicly humiliated.
The One who knows whether church money was handled honestly.
The One who knows whether Scripture was taught faithfully or twisted to protect a reputation.
The One who knows whether leadership was exercised through love or fear.
Suddenly, Hebrews 13:17 becomes far more serious than a convenient verse for demanding obedience.
It becomes a warning against the abuse of spiritual trust.
But we must be equally careful not to turn that truth into an excuse for rejecting all authority.
Because the same Bible that condemns domineering leadership commands believers to respect faithful leaders.
Hebrews 13:7 tells Christians to remember those who spoke the Word of God to them, consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
Notice the emphasis.
Their teaching.
Their conduct.
Their faith.
Not merely their title.
Not merely their popularity.
Not merely their ability to speak powerfully.
Their lives must demonstrate the truth they proclaim.
And Hebrews 13:9 warns believers not to be carried away by strange teachings.
These surrounding verses matter.
Hebrews 13:17 was not written as an isolated slogan that leaders could use whenever someone disagreed with them.
It belongs to a chapter concerned with faithful teaching, Christian perseverance, worship, holiness, and the unchanging identity of Jesus Christ.
Just a few verses earlier, Hebrews 13:8 declares:
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.”
That is the center.
Not the personality of a pastor.
Not the prestige of a denomination.
Not the survival of a ministry brand.
Jesus Christ.
The same Savior who forgives sinners also calls His people to holiness.
The same Lord who commands humility also opposes oppression.
The same Christ who appoints leaders also holds them accountable.
And His authority never becomes less important because a human leader has been given a position in the church.
Consider what happened in Acts 5.
The apostles were commanded by the religious authorities to stop preaching in the name of Jesus.
These were not insignificant people.
They held recognized religious positions.
They possessed institutional authority.
They could impose serious consequences.
Yet Peter and the apostles answered:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” (Acts 5:29, KJV).
The Greek is striking:
Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.
Peitharchein dei theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
“We must obey God rather than human beings.”
The principle is clear.
When human authority commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, obedience to God takes precedence.
This is not permission to disregard every inconvenient instruction from a church leader.
It is a necessary boundary.
No pastor can authorize sin.
No elder can command dishonesty.
No spiritual mentor can require someone to conceal abuse.
No ministry can demand loyalty that belongs to Christ alone.
And no leader can make disobedience to God's Word righteous simply by calling it submission.
But there is another biblical scene we desperately need to remember.
In Acts 17:11, the Bereans received Paul's message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether his teaching was true.
Paul was an apostle.
His calling was extraordinary.
Yet the Bereans were commended for testing what they heard against Scripture.
They did not reject teaching simply because it came from a person in authority.
They listened.
They investigated.
They searched the Scriptures.
Their eagerness and discernment belonged together.
Biblical submission does not require switching off your discernment.
It requires bringing your heart, your questions, and your convictions beneath the authority of God's Word.
That distinction can save a person from years of spiritual confusion.
Because there is a difference between a pastor who says, “Let us examine what Scripture teaches,” and one who says, “You must agree because I am your pastor.”
There is a difference between correction that seeks restoration and humiliation that demands compliance.
There is a difference between protecting the unity of the church and protecting the reputation of someone who has done wrong.
There is a difference between respecting spiritual authority and treating a human being as though he cannot be questioned.
And there is a difference between being difficult to lead and refusing to participate in something sinful.
Sometimes those differences become painfully clear only after trust has been broken.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You once served gladly.
You volunteered when nobody else would.
You gave generously.
You defended your church when others criticized it.
You believed the best about your leaders.
Then something happened.
Maybe you witnessed favoritism.
Maybe you discovered dishonesty.
Maybe you were pressured to remain silent about harmful behavior.
Maybe your private struggles became material for public embarrassment.
Maybe you asked a sincere question and suddenly found yourself treated like an enemy.
And now even hearing the word “submission” makes your chest tighten.
You still love Jesus.
But trusting a church leader again feels frightening.
If that describes you, hear this carefully.
Jesus does not ask you to pretend that evil is good.
He does not require you to deny the truth in order to preserve a leader's image.
And He does not confuse silence with holiness.
The Bible itself contains warnings against corrupt shepherds.
In Ezekiel 34, God rebukes the shepherds of Israel who cared for themselves while neglecting the flock.
They failed to strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, bring back the straying, and seek the lost.
Instead, they ruled harshly.
God did not congratulate them for maintaining authority.
He confronted them.
And He declared His intention to care for His sheep.
In Ezekiel 34:11, the Lord says:
“Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out.” (KJV).
That promise reaches its beautiful fulfillment in the revelation of Jesus as the Good Shepherd.
In John 10:11, Jesus declares:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Read that slowly.
The Good Shepherd gives His life for the sheep.
He does not treat the sheep as disposable sacrifices for his personal ambition.
He sacrifices Himself for them.
That is the difference between the heart of Christ and the spirit of domination.

And when Jesus taught His disciples about leadership in Mark 10:42–45, He contrasted the rulers of the nations, who exercised power over others, with the servant-hearted leadership expected among His followers.
“Whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister.” (Mark 10:43, KJV).
Then He pointed to Himself.
The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Christian leadership must be measured against that cross-shaped standard.
Not celebrity.
Not wealth.
Not the number of followers.
Not the ability to command a room.
Service.
Sacrifice.
Faithfulness.
Truth.
Love.
And accountability before God.
Yet here is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable for another reason.
Some people have genuinely suffered under unhealthy leadership.
Others have never been abused by their pastors, but they call every correction “spiritual abuse” because they do not want anyone confronting their sin.
A pastor lovingly challenges sexual immorality, and someone calls him controlling.
An elder addresses divisive gossip, and someone calls it persecution.
A church insists that its teachers uphold sound doctrine, and someone calls it oppression.
A spiritual mentor urges repentance, and someone accuses that mentor of being judgmental.
We must not confuse biblical correction with abuse.
The same Jesus who protects His sheep also calls them to repent.
The same grace that welcomes sinners teaches them to turn away from ungodliness.
And the same Scripture that restrains abusive leaders calls believers to receive godly instruction with humility.
Hebrews 13:17 still says what it says.
Believers are commanded to obey and submit to their leaders.
That command cannot simply be erased because some leaders have misused it.

When a leader faithfully teaches Scripture, exercises appropriate pastoral oversight, and makes legitimate decisions for the good of the congregation, believers should not automatically resist because of pride, personal preference, or discomfort.
A healthy church cannot function when everyone insists on being accountable only to themselves.
There are times when humility means admitting, “I was wrong.”
There are times when spiritual maturity means receiving correction without becoming defensive.
There are times when love for the body of Christ means accepting a decision that was not your preferred choice.
And there are times when a faithful pastor sees a danger that you have not yet recognized.
That is why godly leadership is a gift.
Not because leaders are perfect.
But because Christ cares for His people through the ministry of faithful servants.
First Thessalonians 5:12–13 urges believers to recognize those who labor among them, lead them in the Lord, and admonish them, and to esteem them highly in love because of their work.
Their work matters.
Their faithfulness matters.
Their spiritual labor matters.
But faithful leaders must also be open to biblical accountability.
In Galatians 2:11–14, Paul publicly confronted Peter when Peter's conduct was not consistent with the truth of the Gospel.
Peter was an apostle.
Yet his position did not make his behavior immune from correction.
This should humble every leader who thinks accountability is disrespect.
And every believer who thinks spiritual authority is inherently evil.
The biblical pattern is neither authoritarianism nor anarchy.
It is a church under the lordship of Jesus Christ, governed by His Word, where leaders serve faithfully and believers respond with humility and discernment.
And when serious allegations arise, the church must respond with truth and justice.
First Timothy 5:19–20 teaches that accusations against elders must be handled with proper evidentiary care and that elders who persist in sin must be rebuked appropriately.
The passage protects against reckless accusations without giving leaders immunity from accountability.
It must never be used to prevent someone from reporting abuse, threats, or criminal conduct to appropriate authorities.
Biblical accountability and lawful protection are not enemies.
And protecting vulnerable people is not rebellion against God.
Now consider another verse frequently used to silence people.
“Touch not mine anointed.” (Psalm 105:15, KJV).
This statement appears in a passage recounting God's protection of His covenant people as they journeyed among nations.
It is not a universal prohibition against questioning pastors, examining doctrine, reporting wrongdoing, or holding church leaders accountable.
To turn it into such a prohibition is to pull the words away from their context.
Anointing does not mean moral perfection.
Calling does not mean immunity.
Spiritual gifting does not cancel the need for integrity.
And a person can speak eloquently about God while behaving in ways that contradict God's commands.
Jesus Himself warned that false prophets could appear in sheep's clothing while inwardly being ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15).
That warning would make little sense if Christians were forbidden from examining those who claim spiritual authority.
In 1 John 4:1, believers are instructed to test the spirits because many false prophets have gone into the world.
And in Matthew 7:16, Jesus teaches that people can be recognized by their fruits.
Discernment is not the enemy of faith.
It is part of faithful obedience.
But discernment must also be honest.
It cannot be driven merely by rumors, resentment, personality conflicts, or the assumption that every imperfect leader is a false shepherd.
Truth requires evidence.
Love refuses slander.
Justice refuses cover-ups.
And holiness refuses to excuse sin simply because the sinner has a microphone.
There is one more detail in Hebrews 13:17 that is often overlooked.
The verse concludes by urging believers to cooperate so that their leaders may carry out their work with joy rather than grief, because grief in that work would be unprofitable for the congregation.
That matters.
Godly pastoral ministry can be exhausting.
A faithful leader may spend years praying for people who never know how much he has carried.
He may visit the sick, counsel struggling marriages, teach Scripture, comfort grieving families, and confront destructive behavior.
He may sacrifice time, energy, and personal comfort because he loves the people entrusted to his care.
Believers should not make that work unnecessarily painful through constant hostility, gossip, selfishness, or refusal to receive sound instruction.
The church should be a place where faithful shepherds can serve with joy.
But the joy of a leader is not purchased by silencing wounded people.
And the grief of a pastor is not automatically proof that the congregation has sinned.
Sometimes leaders grieve because believers resist truth.
Sometimes believers grieve because leaders have betrayed trust.
Both realities deserve biblical honesty.
This is why the Gospel must remain at the center of the conversation.
Because the deepest answer to abusive authority is not simply finding a nicer leader.
And the deepest answer to rebellious independence is not merely finding a stricter church.
We need hearts transformed by Jesus Christ.
We need leaders who have been humbled by the cross.
We need believers who have been softened by grace.
We need churches where repentance is not a slogan preached only to the congregation while the leadership remains untouchable.
We need churches where confession is not weaponized against the vulnerable.
We need churches where forgiveness is never used to pressure people into unsafe situations or to eliminate appropriate consequences.
And we need churches where the Word of God is not treated as a tool for protecting power.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood to create religious empires centered on human personalities.
He came to redeem sinners and gather a people who belong to Him.
Think about Peter.
The disciple who once boldly promised that he would never deny Jesus.
The disciple who failed three times.
The disciple who wept bitterly after his betrayal.
The disciple who knew the shame of discovering that his confidence was greater than his courage.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Christ repeatedly asked Peter whether he loved Him.
And He entrusted Peter with a responsibility.
“Feed my sheep.”
Not “Build your kingdom.”
Not “Make them fear you.”
Not “Protect your image at all costs.”
Feed My sheep.
The sheep still belonged to Jesus.
And the man entrusted with feeding them was himself a forgiven failure.
What a picture of grace.
A fallen disciple restored to service.
A broken man given responsibility.
A shepherd who must never forget that he, too, survives only because of mercy.
That is what spiritual leadership should remember every single day.
The people sitting in the pews are not trophies.
They are souls.
Some arrived carrying grief.
Some are recovering from addiction.
Some are fighting temptations they are ashamed to name.
Some are struggling to believe that God could still love them.
Some are trying to rebuild their faith after religious betrayal.
Some are barely holding on.
And the pastor standing before them is not called to exploit their vulnerability.
He is called to point them to Christ.
But if you are the believer who has been hurt, there is something else you must hear.
Do not allow the failure of a human shepherd to convince you that the Chief Shepherd has abandoned you.
The person who misrepresented Jesus is not Jesus.
The leader who betrayed your trust is not the measure of God's faithfulness.
The church that wounded you does not have the authority to rewrite the character of Christ.
And the pain you experienced does not mean your spiritual future is over.
You may need time to heal.
You may need trustworthy counsel.
You may need to establish boundaries.
You may need to leave an unsafe congregation and find a healthier one.
You may need to report serious wrongdoing.
You may need to relearn what faithful spiritual leadership looks like.
None of those steps automatically means you have rejected Jesus.
But do not mistake healing for permanently closing your heart to every Christian community.
Christ calls His people into fellowship, mutual encouragement, and loving accountability.
There are still faithful pastors.
There are still humble elders.
There are still congregations where Scripture is opened carefully, where questions are welcomed sincerely, where sin is confronted consistently, and where wounded people are treated with dignity.
There are still shepherds who would rather lose their reputation than compromise the truth.
There are still leaders who apologize when they are wrong.
There are still churches where Christ is more important than the person behind the pulpit.
Do not let one person's betrayal become the final chapter of your faith.
And if you are a church leader reading this, perhaps the Holy Spirit is confronting something in you.
Perhaps you have demanded respect without cultivating trust.
Perhaps you have mistaken disagreement for disloyalty.
Perhaps you have used biblical authority to win arguments rather than shepherd hearts.
Perhaps you have been more concerned about protecting your ministry than listening to someone you wounded.
There is grace for repentance.
But repentance must be more than tears in a public statement.
It means acknowledging wrongdoing.
It means turning away from sinful patterns.
It means accepting appropriate accountability.
It means making restitution where possible.
It means recognizing that forgiveness does not automatically restore someone to a position of leadership or remove the consequences of harm.
And sometimes, true repentance means stepping away from authority because the safety of the flock matters more than preserving a title.
That is not the destruction of ministry.
That may be the beginning of genuine obedience to Christ.
Because the Gospel does not exist to preserve our carefully constructed images.
It exposes our sin so that we may come into the light of God's mercy.
The cross tells us two truths we desperately need.
Our sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
And God's love is great enough that Christ willingly came to save sinners.
At Calvary, Jesus did not manipulate people into surrendering their lives for His personal comfort.
He gave Himself for our redemption.
He bore our sins.
He conquered death.
And through His resurrection, He offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why Hebrews 13:17 must never become a weapon that obscures Jesus.
The purpose of faithful spiritual leadership is to help people grow in Christ.
The purpose of biblical submission is not to make believers dependent on a human personality.
It is to encourage humble, orderly, accountable Christian life under the authority of God's Word.
A good shepherd does not become threatened when the sheep learn to recognize the voice of Jesus.
He rejoices.
Because the goal was never to make them follow him instead of Christ.
It was to help them follow Christ more faithfully.
So what should you do when a pastor teaches something you believe is wrong?
Begin with Scripture.
Read the passage in context.
Consider the whole counsel of God.
Ask sincere questions.
Avoid rushing to accusations based on fragments or rumors.
Seek wise counsel from mature believers who are not merely interested in defending a personality.
If the disagreement concerns a legitimate matter of church order or personal preference, practice humility and seek peace.
If it concerns false doctrine, coercion, serious misconduct, or a command to sin, do not surrender your conscience to human authority.
Respond truthfully and wisely.
And where safety is at risk, prioritize protection and appropriate help.
You do not have to choose between honoring God's Word and refusing wrongdoing.
The Bible itself requires both.
Perhaps the most searching question is not simply, “Must I obey my pastor?”
Perhaps it is this:
Am I truly submitted to Jesus Christ?
Because a pastor can demand too much.
And a believer can resist too much.
A leader can become intoxicated with authority.
And a church member can become intoxicated with independence.
Both must kneel before the same Savior.
Both must repent where they have sinned.
Both must receive the same grace.
And both must remember that the Church belongs to Jesus.
Not to the loudest preacher.
Not to the wealthiest donor.
Not to the most influential family.
Not to the most offended member.
Not to the most popular online personality.
To Jesus.
The One who purchased His people with His own blood.
The One who searches hearts.
The One who knows every hidden wound.
The One who sees every secret compromise.
The One who restores the repentant and calls His people to walk in truth.
If this message has touched something you have kept buried, you do not need to pretend that everything is fine.
Perhaps you have been afraid to speak.
Perhaps you have been afraid to trust.
Perhaps you have been resisting correction because of pride.
Perhaps you are a leader who needs to apologize.
Perhaps you are simply tired of seeing Scripture used to divide people who desperately need Jesus.
Whatever your story, bring it honestly before the Lord.
You do not owe strangers the details of your wounds.
God already knows.
And there may be someone reading your simple words who will stop, pray, and remember that they are not the only one struggling.
Not to start another religious argument.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But because someone may be silently wondering whether following Jesus requires surrendering their God-given responsibility to discern truth.
Someone needs to know that the Bible calls us to respect faithful leaders without making them idols.
Someone needs to know that spiritual abuse is not the voice of the Good Shepherd.
And someone needs to know that being corrected by a faithful pastor is not the same thing as being controlled.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown cold, the person searching for answers, and even the skeptic who believes Christianity is nothing more than religious control.
Let them encounter the Jesus who calls sinners to repentance, exposes hypocrisy, forgives the guilty, and restores broken lives.
And if this ministry has helped you understand God's Word more deeply, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.
Not because God withholds His love from those who cannot afford to give.
It is not.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 encourages those who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 describes the generosity of believers who partnered with Paul in Gospel ministry.
Financial support can be a meaningful expression of worship when it flows from gratitude, love, wisdom, and a sincere desire to serve Christ.
A voluntary, recurring ministry offering that helps sustain and expand the creation of biblical articles, devotional teaching, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered encouragement.
For those who wish to set aside a monthly amount as an offering toward this ministry, that support can be a beautiful act of generosity.
It should not, however, be confused with a compulsory biblical tithe or presented as a replacement for responsibilities to your local church, your family, or those in genuine need.
And when many believers each contribute what they can, the ministry can be strengthened to reach more people with the truth of Scripture.
There is also something we want every serious student of God's Word to know.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, prayer, Christian character, spiritual discernment, and a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
They are not reserved only for those who can pay.
They are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible.
It is partnership.

It is the opportunity to help strengthen a ministry committed to teaching Scripture, encouraging repentance, proclaiming grace, and reminding broken people that their story is not beyond the redeeming power of Jesus.
You can still participate meaningfully.
Pray for this ministry.
Read and study the Scriptures.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
And above all, remain faithful to Christ.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build a following that replaces the Church, and certainly not to create another authority that people are afraid to question.
It is to point people to the One whose authority is perfectly righteous, whose mercy is immeasurable, and whose truth can withstand every honest question.
Jesus Christ.
So the next time someone opens Hebrews 13:17 and says, “Obey your leaders and submit to them,” do not dismiss the verse.
Receive its instruction.
Respect faithful shepherds.
Value spiritual accountability.
Remain teachable.
Refuse the arrogance that makes correction impossible.
But also remember the rest of Scripture.
Test teaching by God's Word.
Refuse commands that contradict God's will.
Protect the vulnerable.
Hold leaders to biblical standards.
And never give to a human shepherd the absolute allegiance that belongs to the Chief Shepherd alone.
Because one day, every pastor will lay down his title.
Every elder will surrender his position.
Every congregation will stand before the Lord.
Every hidden motive will be known.
Every act of faithful service will be seen.
And every person who belongs to Christ will discover that the safest place was never beneath the unquestioned authority of a human being.
It was always in the hands of Jesus.
The hands that washed His disciples' feet.
The hands that touched the unclean.
The hands that welcomed the broken.
The hands that were pierced for sinners.
The hands of the Shepherd who did not abandon His sheep when saving them required His own blood.
And perhaps that is what your wounded heart has needed to hear all along.
You can honor faithful leaders without worshiping them.
You can reject spiritual manipulation without rejecting the Church of Jesus Christ.
You can repent of rebellion without surrendering your discernment.
You can forgive without pretending that harm never happened.
And you can begin again, not because people have always represented Christ faithfully, but because Christ Himself remains faithful.
The shepherd who failed you does not get to write the ending of the story that Jesus died to redeem.
